```{python}
    </label>
    <label style="font-size:13px">Judgments per person<br>
      <select id="ex_judg" style="font-size:14px;padding:3px 6px;margin-top:3px"></select>
    </label>
    <div id="ex_read" style="font-size:13px;line-height:1.5"></div>
  </div>
  <svg id="ex_svg" viewBox="0 0 700 330" style="width:100%;height:auto"></svg>
  <p id="ex_note" style="font-size:11.5px;color:#666;margin:2px 0 0"></p>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var D = __PAYLOAD__;
  var svg = document.getElementById('ex_svg'),
      selR = document.getElementById('ex_ratio'),
      selJ = document.getElementById('ex_judg'),
      read = document.getElementById('ex_read'),
      note = document.getElementById('ex_note');
  D.ratios.forEach(function(r){ var o=document.createElement('option');
    o.value=r; o.textContent=r.toFixed(1); if(r===2.5) o.selected=true; selR.appendChild(o); });
  D.judg.forEach(function(j){ var o=document.createElement('option');
    o.value=j; o.textContent=j; if(j===45) o.selected=true; selJ.appendChild(o); });

  var L=58, R=18, T=16, B=44, W=700, H=330;
  var x0=L, x1=W-R, y0=H-B, y1=T;
  var sMin=Math.min.apply(null,D.seps), sMax=Math.max.apply(null,D.seps);
  function px(s){ return x0 + (s-sMin)/(sMax-sMin)*(x1-x0); }
  function py(v){ return y0 - (v/100)*(y0-y1); }
  function el(n,a){ var e=document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg',n);
    for(var k in a) e.setAttribute(k,a[k]); return e; }

  function draw(){
    var r=parseFloat(selR.value), j=parseInt(selJ.value);
    var rows=D.rows.filter(function(d){return d.peak_noise===r && d.judgments===j;})
                   .sort(function(a,b){return a.separation-b.separation;});
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);

    var fx=px(Math.min(D.floor,sMax));
    if(fx>x0) svg.appendChild(el('rect',{x:x0,y:y1,width:fx-x0,height:y0-y1,
      fill:'#999',opacity:0.13}));
    if(fx>x0+8) { var ft=el('text',{x:(x0+fx)/2,y:y1+14,'text-anchor':'middle',
      'font-size':10,fill:'#777'}); ft.textContent='one hump — nothing to detect';
      svg.appendChild(ft); }

    [0,20,40,60,80,100].forEach(function(v){
      svg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:x0,x2:x1,y1:py(v),y2:py(v),
        stroke:'#e4e4e4','stroke-width':1}));
      var t=el('text',{x:x0-8,y:py(v)+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'#555'});
      t.textContent=v+'%'; svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    svg.appendChild(el('line',{x1:x0,x2:x1,y1:py(20),y2:py(20),
      stroke:'#c00','stroke-width':1,'stroke-dasharray':'4 3',opacity:.55}));

    D.seps.forEach(function(s){
      var t=el('text',{x:px(s),y:y0+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'#555'});
      t.textContent=s.toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    var xl=el('text',{x:(x0+x1)/2,y:H-8,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'#333'});
    xl.textContent='neutral-zone width (stars)'; svg.appendChild(xl);

    function series(key,color,label){
      var pts=rows.map(function(d){return px(d.separation)+','+py(d[key]);}).join(' ');
      svg.appendChild(el('polyline',{points:pts,fill:'none',stroke:color,'stroke-width':2.4}));
      rows.forEach(function(d){
        svg.appendChild(el('circle',{cx:px(d.separation),cy:py(d[key]),r:3.6,fill:color}));
      });
      var last=rows[rows.length-1];
      var t=el('text',{x:px(last.separation)-6,y:py(last[key])-9,'text-anchor':'end',
        'font-size':11.5,fill:color,'font-weight':'600'});
      t.textContent=label; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    series('type2','#1f77b4','Type II (missed)');
    series('type1','#d62728','Type I (false alarm)');

    var best=rows.filter(function(d){return d.separation>D.floor && d.type2<=20;});
    read.innerHTML = '<b>At these settings</b><br>' +
      (best.length
        ? 'Type II falls below 20% once the neutral zone reaches <b>'+
          best[0].separation.toFixed(1)+' stars</b>.'
        : 'Type II never falls below 20% at any width shown.');
    note.textContent='Dashed red line marks a 20% Type II error (80% power). '+
      'Each point uses about '+D.n_not2+' people with 0 or 1 reference points and '+
      D.n_is2+' with 2, so the margin is roughly ±5 points.';
  }
  selR.addEventListener('change',draw);
  selJ.addEventListener('change',draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>
"""
    display(HTML(_html.replace('__PAYLOAD__', _payload)))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Notes on the explorer

Set the two dropdowns to whatever your pilot says, then read the **blue** line at
your measured neutral-zone width — that is the fraction of two-reference-point
people you will miss.

Varying **signal vs noise** while holding the other control fixed moves the blue
line considerably further than varying judgments-per-person does. This is the
result established in §2c and §10.1: reducing measurement noise is more effective
than lengthening the survey.
:::


## 6. How many judgments per person?

```{python}
#| label: tbl-required
#| tbl-cap: "Smallest number of judgments per person that gets the FALSE NEGATIVE rate down to 20% (i.e. 80% of two-reference-point people found), and the FALSE POSITIVE rate you pay at that point. Separations with a single-humped true curve are excluded, since there is nothing there to detect."

req = []
for sep, g in sw.groupby('peak separation'):
    if sep <= 2 * PEAK_W:
        continue
    g = g.sort_values('judgments per person')
    ok = g[g['FALSE NEGATIVE: said 0 or 1, truth 2 (%)'] <= 20]
    if len(ok):
        fa = float(ok['FALSE POSITIVE: said 2, truth 0 or 1 (%)'].iloc[0])
        req.append({'peak separation': sep,
                    'judgments needed': int(ok['judgments per person'].iloc[0]),
                    'false positive there (%)': round(fa, 1),
                    'under 10%?': 'yes' if fa <= 10 else 'NO'})
    else:
        req.append({'peak separation': sep,
                    'judgments needed': f'>{max(N_POINTS)}',
                    'false positive there (%)': np.nan, 'under 10%?': '-'})
pd.DataFrame(req).set_index('peak separation') if req else "No resolvable separations in SEP_GRID."
```

## 7. Effect of the number of participants

The error rates are unaffected by the number of participants. This section
documents that result.

The classifier sees one person at a time, so the probability it gets any given
person wrong has nothing to do with how many other people are in your study.
Running 200, 300, 400 and 500 participants should give you the *same* underlying
rates, differing only by chance.

What does change is the **error bar**. With more people you are measuring the
same rate more precisely. The last column shows the 95% margin of error on the
false-negative row, which shrinks roughly like one over the square root of the
number of truly-bimodal people.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-n-robust
#| tbl-cap: "Error rates at four participant counts, holding judgments per person and peak separation fixed. The rates should wander only within the margin of error shown in the last column -- if they do, sample size is not affecting them, which is the expected and correct result."

N_ROBUST_NPT = 30
rows = []
for sep in [s for s in SEP_GRID if s > 2 * PEAK_W][:2] or SEP_GRID[-1:]:
    for n_ppl in N_PEOPLE_GRID:
        pop = simulate_population(n_ppl, N_ROBUST_NPT, sep)
        pr = classify_population(pop)
        fp_r, fn_r = ref_rates(pr)
        n_bi = n_ppl * SHAPE_MIX['bimodal']
        rows.append({
            'peak separation': sep,
            'n people': n_ppl,
            'false negative (%)': round(fn_r, 1),
            'false positive (%)': round(fp_r, 1),
            'margin of error (+/- pp)': round(1.96 * np.sqrt(.25 / n_bi) * 100, 1),
        })
n_rob = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(['peak separation', 'n people'])
print(f"{N_ROBUST_NPT} judgments per person throughout.\n")
n_rob
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-n-robust
#| fig-cap: "The same numbers as a picture. Points are the estimated rates; bars are the 95% margin of error. Flat lines within overlapping bars mean the rate is a property of the method and the per-person data, not of how many participants you run."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6

d = n_rob.reset_index()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharex=True)
for (sep, g), col in zip(d.groupby('peak separation'), ['#1f77b4', '#d62728']):
    for ax, metric in zip(axes, ['false negative (%)', 'false positive (%)']):
        ax.errorbar(g['n people'], g[metric], yerr=g['margin of error (+/- pp)'],
                    marker='o', ms=5, capsize=4, color=col, label=f'sep {sep}')
for ax, t in zip(axes, ['False negative: bimodal people missed',
                        'False positive: unimodal called bimodal']):
    ax.set_title(t, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel('number of participants')
    ax.set_xticks(N_PEOPLE_GRID)
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylabel('%')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The role of sample size

None of this says 500 participants is pointless. It says participants buy you
different things than judgments-per-person do:

- **Judgments per person** buy you a lower error rate on each individual call.
- **Participants** buy you precision on the *population* questions — what
  fraction of people have a neutral zone, and where the boundaries sit on
  average. Those are the questions your study is actually about.

So set judgments-per-person from §6 and set participants from whatever precision
you need on the population estimate.
:::

## 8. Fidelity to the real experiment

Every row below is an assumption baked into Layers 1 and 2. The right-hand column
is what happens to the reported error rates if the assumption is wrong.

| # | Assumption in the code | Real experiment? | If it is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.1 | Peaks are exactly bell-shaped, and the classifier fits bell shapes | Unknowable in advance | Tested in 8.1 below — turns out to cost almost nothing |
| 8.2 | Noise is symmetric, unbiased, same size at every x | Sliders are usually noisier in the middle | False positives rise where noise is largest |
| 8.3 | A person's responses are independent of one another | Order effects, drift and fatigue are real | **Biggest risk.** Correlated noise looks exactly like a bump |
| 8.4 | Midpoints are evenly spaced and identical for everyone | True only if your design is fixed, not randomised | Uneven spacing leaves gaps that invite spurious peaks |
| 8.5 | Each midpoint is asked once (`REPS = 1`) | Your call | Repeats average out noise; 2 reps is worth about a 40% noise cut |
| 8.6 | Baseline is flat under the peaks (`BASE_SLOPE = 0`) | Weber's law says probably not | A tilted baseline makes one peak look taller than the other |
| 8.7 | Slider values are clipped at 0 and 100 | Yes | Only bites if `BASELINE` sits within about 2 SD of an end |

### 8.1 Sensitivity to the assumed peak shape

The check: generate participants whose peaks are **not** bell-shaped — triangular
instead — and fit them with the bell-shaped classifier. Any gap between the two
rows is the cost of misspecification.

At the defaults the two rows come out **the same to within Monte Carlo error**,
which is genuinely reassuring: at this noise level the classifier is deciding
*how many humps there are*, not *what precise shape they have*, so getting the
peak shape wrong costs almost nothing. Do re-run this if you lower `SLIDER_SD`,
because a sharper signal makes the fit fussier about shape.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-misspec
#| tbl-cap: "Same classifier, two different truths. 'Gaussian peaks' matches what the classifier assumes; 'triangular peaks' does not. A gap between the rows is what model misspecification would cost you."

def _tri(x, m, w):
    """Triangular bump of height 1 -- deliberately NOT the shape we fit."""
    return np.clip(1 - np.abs(x - m) / (2.0 * w), 0, None)

def simulate_person_shape(shape, n_points, sep, bump_fn):
    p = draw_person_params(shape, sep)
    x = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, n_points)
    if shape == 'unimodal':
        y = _base(x) + p['amp'] * bump_fn(x, p['loc'], PEAK_W)
    elif shape == 'bimodal':
        y = _base(x) + p['amp'] * (bump_fn(x, p['loc1'], PEAK_W)
                                   + bump_fn(x, p['loc2'], PEAK_W))
    else:
        y = true_curve(x, shape, p)
    return x, np.clip(y + rng.normal(0, SLIDER_SD, x.size), 0, SLIDER_MAX)

MIS_SEP, MIS_NPT, MIS_N = 1.0, 30, 300
mis = []
for label, fn in [('gaussian peaks (matches the fit)', _bump),
                  ('triangular peaks (does not)', _tri)]:
    pairs = []
    for shape in ('unimodal', 'bimodal'):
        for _ in range(MIS_N):
            x, y = simulate_person_shape(shape, MIS_NPT, MIS_SEP, fn)
            pairs.append((shape, classify_shape(x, y)[0]))
    cm = confusion_from_pairs(pairs)
    mis.append({'truth generated as': label,
                'bimodal found (%)': round(cell(cm, 'bimodal', 'bimodal'), 1),
                'false bimodal (%)': round(cell(cm, 'unimodal', 'bimodal'), 1)})
print(f"{MIS_N} people per shape, {MIS_NPT} judgments, separation {MIS_SEP}\n")
pd.DataFrame(mis).set_index('truth generated as')
```

### 8.3 Correlated responses within a participant

This is the assumption most likely to be violated and least likely to be noticed.
The code adds a fresh, independent random number to every dot. A real participant
drifts: if they are running high on trial 7 they are probably still running high
on trial 8. Drift produces smooth wiggles in the data that are **indistinguishable
from a real bump** by any method that only sees one person's dots.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Independent noise (what the file assumes) against drifting noise of the SAME total size. Nothing about the person changed -- only how their errors are correlated across trials."

def simulate_person_ar(shape, n_points, sep, rho):
    """Same person, same total noise, but errors drift with correlation rho."""
    p = draw_person_params(shape, sep)
    x = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, n_points)
    e = np.empty(n_points)
    e[0] = rng.normal(0, SLIDER_SD)
    s = SLIDER_SD * np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2)       # keeps the marginal SD at SLIDER_SD
    for i in range(1, n_points):
        e[i] = rho * e[i - 1] + rng.normal(0, s)
    return x, np.clip(true_curve(x, shape, p) + e, 0, SLIDER_MAX)

corr = []
for rho in (0.0, 0.3, 0.6):
    pairs = []
    for shape in ('unimodal', 'bimodal', 'flat'):
        for _ in range(250):
            x, y = simulate_person_ar(shape, MIS_NPT, MIS_SEP, rho)
            pairs.append((shape, classify_shape(x, y)[0]))
    cm = confusion_from_pairs(pairs)
    corr.append({'trial-to-trial correlation': rho,
                 'bimodal found (%)': round(cell(cm, 'bimodal', 'bimodal'), 1),
                 'unimodal called bimodal (%)': round(cell(cm, 'unimodal', 'bimodal'), 1),
                 'FLAT called bimodal (%)': round(cell(cm, 'flat', 'bimodal'), 1)})
pd.DataFrame(corr).set_index('trial-to-trial correlation')
```

The `flat` row is the one to read. Those people have **no structure whatsoever**
in their true curve. Every bimodal call in that row is the method inventing a
neutral zone out of pure noise. If that number climbs as correlation rises, your
real-world false-positive rate is higher than the headline tables say.

The practical defence is design, not analysis: **randomise the order** in which
midpoints are presented for each participant. Drift then smears across the x-axis
instead of pooling into a fake bump.

## 9. Summary of findings

```{python}
#| label: summary

resolvable = [s for s in SEP_GRID if s > 2 * PEAK_W]
print(f"Peak half-width is {PEAK_W}, so separations at or below {2*PEAK_W:.1f} stars "
      f"are single-humped curves with nothing to detect.")
print(f"Resolvable separations in this run: {resolvable}\n")
print("At the largest number of judgments in the sweep:\n")
print(f"  {'sep':>5}{'FALSE POS (said 2, truth 0/1)':>32}"
      f"{'FALSE NEG (said 0/1, truth 2)':>32}")
for sep, g in sw.groupby('peak separation'):
    b = g.sort_values('judgments per person').iloc[-1]
    tag = '' if sep > 2 * PEAK_W else '   [true curve has ONE hump]'
    print(f"  {sep:>5}{b['FALSE POSITIVE: said 2, truth 0 or 1 (%)']:>32.1f}"
          f"{b['FALSE NEGATIVE: said 0 or 1, truth 2 (%)']:>32.1f}{tag}")
```

Four things these tables are telling you.

**Peak separation matters more than anything else, and below `2 * PEAK_W` the
question is malformed.** Peaks closer together than twice the peak width are not
two peaks; they are one. No amount of data recovers a structure that is not
there. Decide what separation you actually care about detecting before reading
any other table.

**Participants do not change the error rates.** §7 shows the rates flat across
200 to 500 people. Judgments per person is the knob that moves them.

**The false-positive rate is the binding constraint, and more data does not fix
it.** The bimodal shape always has spare flexibility to chase noise, so some
genuinely unimodal people will always be labelled bimodal. Across several hundred
participants that is enough to manufacture a "two reference point" subgroup that
does not exist.

**So classify with a caveat, not a verdict.** Two protections, both of which use
the fact that you have hundreds of people:

- **Report the fitted neutral-zone width alongside the label**, rather than only
  the label. Note from §3c that this is a *description*, not a second test —
  thresholding the width or the trough depth is markedly worse than BIC at
  deciding who has two reference points.
- **Fit all participants jointly in a hierarchical model**, letting peak
  locations and amplitudes come from population-level distributions. Shrinkage is
  exactly what suppresses false bimodal calls.

Then do the thing you actually want: **among people classified bimodal, ask where
their peaks fall** and check those against that person's separately elicited
boundaries. `classify_shape` already returns the fitted locations as its second
value.

## 10. Nonparametric alternative

If assuming a bell-shaped peak is a concern, here is a distribution-free version:
fit the best **unimodal regression** — which assumes only "rises then falls", no
functional form — then bootstrap its residuals to get the null distribution of
the peak count. Unlike Hartigan's dip, it is calibrated for *your* design and
sample size.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The smoothing bandwidth controls power, not the false-positive rate

The bootstrap generates its null using the same smoother, so any tendency of a
narrow bandwidth to see spurious peaks appears in the null too and cancels out.
Measured across bandwidths from 0.03 to 0.18 at peak/noise 4:

- **false-positive rate stayed at 0-3% throughout** — that is what the
  calibration buys, and it is robust to how you smooth
- **detection swung from 0% to 37%**, peaking sharply at `frac = 0.06`

The smoother family barely matters (gaussian 35%, local-linear 37%) but a plain
moving average is much worse (7%). `frac = 0.06` is near optimal *for peaks 0.9
stars apart* — the bandwidth must sit at roughly a quarter of the separation you
want to resolve; changing `PEAK_SEP` requires retuning `frac`, or power collapses
silently.
:::

```{python}
#| label: nonparametric

def unimodal_regression(y):
    """Best rises-then-falls fit. Nonparametric."""
    n = len(y); idx = np.arange(n)
    inc, dec = IsotonicRegression(increasing=True), IsotonicRegression(increasing=False)
    best, best_rss = None, np.inf
    for m in range(n):
        f = np.empty(n)
        f[:m + 1] = inc.fit_transform(idx[:m + 1], y[:m + 1])
        if m < n - 1:
            f[m:] = dec.fit_transform(idx[m:], y[m:])
        rss = float(np.sum((y - f) ** 2))
        if rss < best_rss:
            best_rss, best = rss, f
    return best

def _smooth(x, y, frac):
    # The bandwidth must sit well BELOW the peak separation you want to resolve.
    # At frac=0.18 the smoother merged peaks 0.9 stars apart even with zero noise.
    h = frac * (x.max() - x.min())
    K = np.exp(-0.5 * ((x[:, None] - x[None, :]) / h) ** 2)
    return (K @ y) / K.sum(axis=1)

def count_peaks(x, y, frac=0.06, prom_frac=0.10):
    s = _smooth(x, y, frac)
    r = float(np.ptp(s))
    return 0 if r <= 0 else len(find_peaks(s, prominence=prom_frac * r)[0])

def classify_nonparametric(x, y, B=99, alpha=.05, frac=0.06, prom_frac=0.10):
    """Bootstrap-calibrated peak count."""
    obs = count_peaks(x, y, frac, prom_frac)
    if obs < 2:
        return 'unimodal', ()            # short-circuit: the p-value cannot rescue it
    fit = unimodal_regression(y)
    resid = y - fit
    resid = resid - resid.mean()
    null = np.array([count_peaks(x, fit + rng.choice(resid, len(y), replace=True),
                                 frac, prom_frac)
                     for _ in range(B)])
    p = (1 + np.sum(null >= obs)) / (B + 1)
    return ('bimodal' if p < alpha else 'unimodal'), ()

if RUN_NONPARAMETRIC:
    np_rows = []
    for npt in [30, 60, 90]:
        pop = simulate_population(80, npt, 1.0,
                                  mix={'unimodal': 0.5, 'bimodal': 0.5})
        cm = confusion(pop, classify_nonparametric)
        np_rows.append({'judgments per person': npt,
                        'bimodal correct (%)': cell(cm, 'bimodal', 'bimodal'),
                        'unimodal called bimodal (%)': cell(cm, 'unimodal', 'bimodal')})
    display(pd.DataFrame(np_rows).set_index('judgments per person').round(1))
else:
    print("RUN_NONPARAMETRIC is False (it runs a bootstrap per simulated person).")
    print("Set it True in the config block to reproduce these reference values,")
    print("measured separately with peaks 0.9 stars apart:\n")
    print("  peak/noise = 4:  60 judgments -> 33% found;  80 -> 48%;  120 -> 71%")
    print("  peak/noise = 6:  60 judgments -> 76% found;  80 -> 89%;  120 -> 96%")
    print("  false-bimodal rate throughout: 0-1%")
```

### 10.1 Sensitivity of the nonparametric test to sample size

The statistic in `classify_nonparametric` is an **integer** — a count of peaks.
Integer statistics give lumpy, conservative p-values and throw away information:
a barely-there second peak and an obvious one both score "2". Replacing it with a
**continuous** statistic — the prominence of the second peak as a fraction of the
curve's range — while changing nothing else lifts detection enormously.

That continuous version runs a Type I error of 7-13% rather than the nominal 5%,
because the isotonic null **overfits**: its residuals come out too small, so the
bootstrap null is too tight. Rescaling residuals by the fit's effective degrees
of freedom ("corrected" below) fixes the calibration at a cost in detection.

The sweep below was run separately by `np_sweep_nonparametric.py` (about 12
minutes) and its output is in `np_sweep_results.csv`. Re-run that script if you
change any Layer 1 parameter.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-np-sweep
#| tbl-cap: "Type I and Type II error of the CONTINUOUS nonparametric test at 40, 45 and 50 judgments per person. 200 simulated people per cell, so the margin of error is +/- 3.0 points on Type I and +/- 6.9 on Type II. Read across a row: extra judgments do almost nothing. Read down: separation and signal strength dominate."

import os
if os.path.exists('np_sweep_results.csv'):
    npsw = pd.read_csv('np_sweep_results.csv')
    t = npsw.pivot_table(index=['peak/noise', 'separation', 'judgments'],
                         columns='version', values=['Type I (%)', 'Type II (%)'])
    t = t[[('Type I (%)', 'uncorrected'), ('Type II (%)', 'uncorrected'),
           ('Type I (%)', 'corrected'),   ('Type II (%)', 'corrected')]]
    t.columns = ['Type I uncorr', 'Type II uncorr', 'Type I corr', 'Type II corr']
    display(t)
else:
    print("np_sweep_results.csv not found - run np_sweep_nonparametric.py first.")
```

**Two things to take from this.**

*Extra judgments buy nothing in this range.* At peak/noise 4 and separation 1.0
the Type II error goes 30.5 → 31.5 → 19.0 as you move from 40 to 50 judgments,
which is inside the error bars. You are on a plateau. Separation and signal
strength swamp sample size: dropping separation from 1.0 to 0.8 stars pushes
Type II from 19% to 83%.

*And it still loses to BIC.* At the default signal strength, with separation 1.0:

| method | judgments per person | Type I | Type II |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BIC** (§3b) | **30** | **5.0%** | **27%** |
| nonparametric, corrected | 50 | 4.0% | 49% |

BIC wins on both error types with 20 fewer judgments per person — while solving
the harder problem, since it chooses among four shapes rather than two. The
nonparametric route's whole appeal was tight false-positive control, and BIC
already delivers that.

::: {.callout-note}
## Relevance of this section

Because it tells you where your leverage is. The plateau means lengthening the
survey is a dead end. The columns say the two things that matter are **peak
separation** (a fact about people, which §2 shows you cannot measure below
`2 * PEAK_W`) and **`PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD`** (partly under your control).

Moving from the 2.5 row to the 4.0 row is worth far more than twenty extra
judgments — and unlike separation, you can buy it: quieter measurement through
repeated ratings per midpoint, a practice block, or a forced-choice response
format instead of a slider.
:::

**The trade-off.** The nonparametric route has excellent false-positive
control — around 1%, against 10-25% for the AICc classifier — but needs roughly
**80 judgments per person** to find 80% of bimodal people, and more when the
signal is weaker. It buys honesty with sample size. Which you prefer depends on
whether a false neutral zone or a missed one is worse for your argument.


## 11. An alternative experimental design

Every number so far says the same thing: **80% detection is hard to reach in this
design, and adding judgments does not get you there.** That is worth taking
seriously as a signal about the design rather than about the analysis.

### Why the present design has limited power

The current task measures a **difference** between two nearby ratings. But a
discriminability peak is not the boundary itself — it is the *steepest part* of
the underlying categorisation. In other words, this design measures something
like the **derivative** of the thing you actually care about, and then asks the
classifier to recover the original from it.

Recovering a function from noisy measurements of its slope is much harder than
measuring the function directly. That is the whole difficulty, and it also
explains the §2 resolution floor: two peaks closer than `2 * PEAK_W` merge into
one hump, so the design is **structurally blind** below that separation, no
matter how much data you collect.

### Direct estimation of the boundaries

Ask two binary questions about a **single** rating, rather than a slider about a
pair:

- *"Would you consider buying this?"* — the answer flips at the **lower** boundary
- *"Would you avoid this?"* — the answer flips at the **upper** boundary

Each question gives a standard psychometric function, and its flip point is a
boundary estimated directly. Then:

- **one reference point** ⟺ the two flip points **coincide**
- **two reference points** ⟺ they are separated, and the gap *is* the neutral zone

This is no longer a question about humps. It is a question about whether two
thresholds differ, which is among the best-understood measurements in
psychophysics.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-design-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Head-to-head at equal total judgments per person, both scored with BIC. Design A is the current slider-on-pairs task; Design B is the two-binary-questions task. 200 simulated people per cell, so the margin of error is about +/- 6.9 points."

from scipy.optimize import minimize

PSY_SLOPE, PSY_LAPSE = 0.18, 0.03    # boundary fuzziness (stars) and misclick rate

def _logi(x, m, sl):
    z = np.clip(-(x - m) / max(sl, 1e-6), -500, 500)   # clip to avoid exp overflow
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(z))

def simB(shape, n, sep, slope=None):
    """n total judgments, split evenly between the two questions."""
    slope = PSY_SLOPE if slope is None else slope
    c = PEAK_CENTRE + rng.normal(0, PEAK_LOC_SD)
    t_lo, t_hi = (c, c) if shape == 'unimodal' else (c - sep / 2, c + sep / 2)
    m = n // 2
    x = np.linspace(MID_LO, MID_HI, m)
    p_con = PSY_LAPSE + (1 - 2 * PSY_LAPSE) * _logi(x, t_lo, slope)
    p_avo = PSY_LAPSE + (1 - 2 * PSY_LAPSE) * (1 - _logi(x, t_hi, slope))
    return x, (rng.random(m) < p_con).astype(int), (rng.random(m) < p_avo).astype(int)

def _nllB(x, rc, ra, t_lo, t_hi, sl):
    pc = np.clip(PSY_LAPSE + (1 - 2 * PSY_LAPSE) * _logi(x, t_lo, sl), 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)
    pa = np.clip(PSY_LAPSE + (1 - 2 * PSY_LAPSE) * (1 - _logi(x, t_hi, sl)), 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)
    return -(np.sum(rc * np.log(pc) + (1 - rc) * np.log(1 - pc))
             + np.sum(ra * np.log(pa) + (1 - ra) * np.log(1 - pa)))

def testB(x, rc, ra):
    """BIC: do the two thresholds differ, or are they one and the same?"""
    n = 2 * len(x)
    one = minimize(lambda q: _nllB(x, rc, ra, q[0], q[0], q[1]),
                   [PEAK_CENTRE, PSY_SLOPE], method='Nelder-Mead',
                   options={'maxiter': 3000, 'fatol': 1e-6})
    two = minimize(lambda q: _nllB(x, rc, ra, min(q[0], q[1]), max(q[0], q[1]), q[2]),
                   [PEAK_CENTRE - .3, PEAK_CENTRE + .3, PSY_SLOPE],
                   method='Nelder-Mead', options={'maxiter': 5000, 'fatol': 1e-6})
    return (2 * two.fun + 3 * np.log(n)) < (2 * one.fun + 2 * np.log(n))

def testA(x, y):
    """Design A, restricted to the same two-way question for a fair comparison."""
    sc = {}
    for nm in ('unimodal', 'bimodal'):
        fn, k, bnds = candidates(x)[nm]
        try:
            po, _ = curve_fit(fn, x, y, p0=_p0(x, y, nm), bounds=bnds,
                              maxfev=FIT_MAXFEV, ftol=FIT_TOL, xtol=FIT_TOL)
            sc[nm] = info_criterion(float(np.sum((y - fn(x, *po)) ** 2)), len(x), k)
        except Exception:
            sc[nm] = np.inf
    return sc['bimodal'] < sc['unimodal']

DES_NPER = 200
des_rows = []
for sep in (0.4, 0.8, 1.0):
    for npt in (30, 45):
        fa = np.mean([testA(*simulate_person('unimodal', npt, sep)[:2])
                      for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
        pa = np.mean([testA(*simulate_person('bimodal', npt, sep)[:2])
                      for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
        fb = np.mean([testB(*simB('unimodal', npt, sep)) for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
        pb = np.mean([testB(*simB('bimodal', npt, sep)) for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
        des_rows.append({'separation': sep, 'judgments': npt,
                         'A Type I (%)': round(100 * fa, 1),
                         'A Type II (%)': round(100 * (1 - pa), 1),
                         'B Type I (%)': round(100 * fb, 1),
                         'B Type II (%)': round(100 * (1 - pb), 1)})
pd.DataFrame(des_rows).set_index(['separation', 'judgments'])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-design-b-slope
#| tbl-cap: "Design B has its own master parameter, exactly as Design A has PEAK_AMP/SLIDER_SD: the width of the neutral zone relative to how FUZZY each boundary is. Cells are Type II error (two-reference-point people missed) at 45 judgments. Type I stays near 5% throughout, which is the point -- the test stays honest even where it lacks power."

slope_rows = []
for slope in (0.10, 0.18, 0.30, 0.45):
    r = {'boundary fuzziness (stars)': slope}
    for sep in (0.4, 0.8, 1.0):
        pb = np.mean([testB(*simB('bimodal', 45, sep, slope=slope))
                      for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
        r[f'sep {sep}'] = round(100 * (1 - pb), 1)
    fb = np.mean([testB(*simB('unimodal', 45, 1.0, slope=slope))
                  for _ in range(DES_NPER)])
    r['Type I (%)'] = round(100 * fb, 1)
    slope_rows.append(r)
pd.DataFrame(slope_rows).set_index('boundary fuzziness (stars)')
```

### Results of the comparison

**Design B dominates at equal cost.** At separation 0.8 and 45 judgments it cuts
the Type II error from roughly 44% to about 10% — clearing the 80% power bar that
Design A never reaches — while holding Type I nearer 5%.

**It has no resolution floor.** Design A is structurally blind below
`2 * PEAK_W` = 0.6 stars, where two peaks are literally one hump. Design B still
detects a 0.4-star neutral zone, because two thresholds 0.4 apart are perfectly
estimable even though two *peaks* 0.4 apart do not exist. **That floor was an
artefact of measuring pairs, not a fact about perception.**

**But it has its own master parameter,** and it must be piloted just as
`PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD` must be. If boundaries are very fuzzy — a transition
spread over 0.45 stars — Design B loses most of its advantage and can do slightly
worse than Design A at wide separations. What survives at every fuzziness level
is the well-behaved Type I error.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Trade-off between the two designs

These are different constructs, and a reviewer will say so. Design A measures
**perceptual discriminability** — an indirect, implicit signature that is hard to
fake. Design B measures **declared category membership**, which is far better
powered but more open to introspection and demand effects.

The strongest study runs **both**: Design B as the well-powered primary measure
of where the boundaries are, and Design A on a subset as convergent evidence that
those boundaries show up in perception too. `classify_shape` already returns the
fitted peak locations, so the two can be compared person by person.
:::



## 12. Does the size of the rating scale matter?

Short answer: **no, not by itself.** A 5-point scale, a 10-point scale and a
0-100 scale give you the same error rates, because nothing in this analysis
depends on absolute units — only on **ratios**.

### Scale invariance

Below, four different scales are set up with the *same* proportions: the tested
window is 75% of the full range, the peak half-width is 10% of the window, and
the neutral zone is 27% of the window. If scale size mattered, these rows would
differ.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scale-invariance
#| tbl-cap: "Four scales, identical ratios, 45 judgments per person. 300 simulated people per cell, so the margin of error is about +/- 5.7 points. The rows agree, which is the point: the absolute units cancel out."

import os
if os.path.exists('scale_invariance.csv'):
    display(pd.read_csv('scale_invariance.csv').set_index('scale'))
else:
    print("Run scale_size_analysis.py first.")
```

### Measured neutral zones as a fraction of range

This is the useful part. Expressed as a fraction of each scale's full range,
the widths you measured are nearly identical:

| scale | full range | neutral zone | **% of range** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-5 stars | 4 | 0.6 - 0.8 | **15 - 20%** |
| 1-6 points | 5 | 0.8 | **16%** |
| 1-10 points | 9 | 1.8 | **20%** |
| 0-100 | 100 | 20 | **20%** |

People are carving the scale into the same *proportions* whatever its length.
So **all four of your scales are the same experiment**, and switching between
them cannot change your power. Changing scale is not a lever.

### The governing ratio

Two bumps of half-width `w` produce two humps only when their centres are more
than `2w` apart (§2). So the quantity that governs detectability is

**neutral zone width ÷ (2 × peak half-width)**

and it must exceed 1 for a second peak to exist at all. The table below fixes
the neutral zone at your measured values and sweeps the peak half-width, both as
a percentage of the full scale range.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scalefree-power
#| tbl-cap: "Scale-free power. Both the neutral zone and the peak half-width are expressed as a percentage of the FULL scale range, so this table applies to every scale you might use. Type I here is the hardest of the three false-positive routes -- one-reference-point people called two -- so it runs above the pooled figure in section 5."

if os.path.exists('scalefree_power.csv'):
    sf = pd.read_csv('scalefree_power.csv')
    display(sf.pivot_table(
        index=['neutral zone (% of range)', 'peak half-width (% of range)',
               'NZ / (2 x peak w)', 'two humps exist?'],
        columns='judgments', values=['Type I (%)', 'Type II (%)']))
else:
    print("Run scale_size_analysis.py first.")
```

The `NZ / (2 x peak w)` column governs the result. Below 1 there is no second hump and the
Type II error is 80-90% no matter what else you do. Around 1.2 it is still 45-62%.
You need roughly **2 or above** before the Type II error drops under 20%.

With a neutral zone of 17.5% of range, that means a peak half-width of about
**4% of the range or less**. The document's default (`PEAK_W = 0.30` on a 1-5
scale, which is 7.5% of the range) sits at a ratio of about 1.2 — squarely in
the region where you miss most of the people you are looking for.

::: {.callout-important}
## An unmeasured quantity

You have good estimates of the **neutral zone width**. You have no estimate of
the **peak half-width**, and the table above says that is now the single most
important unknown in the whole design. Everything else is settled.

Estimate it from pilot data the same way as `PEAK_AMP / SLIDER_SD`: fit the
unimodal shape to 20-30 pilot participants and read off the fitted `w`. If it
comes out near 4% of your scale range you are in good shape at 45 judgments. If
it comes out near 7% or more, this task cannot answer your question at any
sample size, and §11 is the way forward.
:::

### Rating granularity

Absolute units cancel, but the number of **distinct rating values** does not. A
1-5 scale rated to the nearest half-point offers only 7 usable midpoints in the
tested window; a 0-100 scale offers as many as you like.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scale-granularity
#| tbl-cap: "Same neutral zone, same peak width, same 45 judgments -- only the coarseness of the rating scale differs. Coarse scales repeat midpoints rather than adding new ones."

if os.path.exists('scale_granularity.csv'):
    display(pd.read_csv('scale_granularity.csv').set_index('rating granularity'))
else:
    print("Run scale_size_analysis.py first.")
```

This matters far less than you might expect. Once you have **about 13 distinct
midpoints** the error rates stop moving — 0.25, 0.1, 0.05 and fully continuous
all land within the margin of error of one another. Only the very coarsest case
collapses: 7 distinct midpoints cannot describe a two-humped curve at all, and
the Type II error goes to 100%.

So the granularity rule is a floor, not a gradient: **make sure your design
yields at least ~15 distinct pair midpoints, and beyond that stop worrying about
it.** On a 1-5 star scale, rating to the nearest 0.25 is already enough.

### Summary

1. **Switching scales does not change the error rates.** All four measured scales
   are equivalent under the simulation.
2. **The binding unknown is peak half-width relative to the scale range**, not
   the scale itself. Measure it in the pilot.
3. **Granularity only needs to clear a low bar** — about 15 distinct midpoints.
4. If the pilot puts the peak half-width above roughly 5-6% of range, the
   ratio falls below 1.5 and no amount of data rescues this design. That is the
   point at which to adopt the direct-boundary task in §11, which has no such
   floor.


::: {.callout-warning}
## Why not Hartigan's dip test

Dip takes a **sample of values** and asks whether their density has one hump.
Your data are `(midpoint, slider response)` pairs — a **curve**, whose humps are
peaks of a function, not of a density. The midpoints are fixed by your design
rather than drawn from a distribution, so there is nothing for dip to test.

**What actually happens if you try.** Two routes, both checked on noiseless
curves so that nothing is blamed on noise:

*Route 1 — feed it the slider values.* This asks whether people's **ratings**
cluster, which can look bimodal purely from scale use (lots of 0s and 100s). It
says nothing whatever about **where on the star scale** the peaks sit, which is
the entire question. Wrong object, so the numbers do not matter.

*Route 2 — build a pseudo-sample* by replicating each midpoint in proportion to
its slider response, then dip that. This is the tempting one, and it is
**density-dependent in a way that disqualifies it**:

| midpoints on the grid | 1-peak curve | 2-peak curve (sep 0.9) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2001 (unrealistically dense) | D = 0.001, p = 1.00 | D = 0.027, p < .0001 | works |
| **20 (your actual design)** | D = 0.097, **p < .000001** | D = 0.060, **p < .000001** | **both "bimodal"** |

At a dense grid it does the right thing. At **20 midpoints it calls everything
bimodal**, including a curve with one peak, because the pseudo-sample is 20
distinct values repeated thousands of times and the **ties drive the statistic**
rather than the shape. Worse, D is *larger* for the one-peak curve (0.097) than
for the two-peak curve (0.060) — so it is not merely noisy, it is pointing the
wrong way.

You cannot fix this by adding midpoints, because the density you would need is
far beyond what a participant can sit through.

Dip is fine for genuine distributions — for instance, whether the population
distribution of perceived midpoints is bimodal across people. There, remember to
**jitter**: on rounded data, ties alone moved a real dataset from p = .047 to
p = .53.
:::
